      23             : // Data management for potential rvalue conversions from Python to C++
      24             : // types. When a client requests a conversion to T* or T&, we
      25             : // generally require that an object of type T exists in the source
      26             : // Python object, and the code here does not apply**. This implements
      27             : // conversions which may create new temporaries of type T. The classic
      28             : // example is a conversion which converts a Python tuple to a
      29             : // std::vector. Since no std::vector lvalue exists in the Python
      30             : // object -- it must be created "on-the-fly" by the converter, and
      31             : // which must manage the lifetime of the created object.
      32             : //
      33             : // Note that the client is not precluded from using a registered
      34             : // lvalue conversion to T in this case. In other words, we will
      35             : // happily accept a Python object which /does/ contain a std::vector
      36             : // lvalue, provided an appropriate converter is registered. So, while
      37             : // this is an rvalue conversion from the client's point-of-view, the
      38             : // converter registry may serve up lvalue or rvalue conversions for
      39             : // the target type.
      40             : //
      41             : // ** C++ argument from_python conversions to T const& are an
      42             : // exception to the rule for references: since in C++, const
      43             : // references can bind to temporary rvalues, we allow rvalue
      44             : // converters to be chosen when the target type is T const& for some
      45             : // T.

      48             : // Conversions begin by filling in and returning a copy of this
      49             : // structure. The process looks up a converter in the rvalue converter
      50             : // registry for the target type. It calls the convertible() function
      51             : // of each registered converter, passing the source PyObject* as an
      52             : // argument, until a non-null result is returned. This result goes in
      53             : // the convertible field, and the converter's construct() function is
      54             : // stored in the construct field.
      55             : //
      56             : // If no appropriate converter is found, conversion fails and the
      57             : // convertible field is null. When used in argument conversion for
      58             : // wrapped C++ functions, it causes overload resolution to reject the
      59             : // current function but not to fail completely. If an exception is
      60             : // thrown, overload resolution stops and the exception propagates back
